title: BARC-Bench: Benign Asks, Risky Consequences
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026]
Title:BARC-Bench: Benign Asks, Risky Consequences
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Task instructions from users for agents are inherently underspecified, especially regarding safety boundaries--creating behavioral risks. To study these risks, we introduce BARC-Bench, a collection of 110 tasks across nine simulated workspace environments where benign requests leave openings for unsafe actions. In this benchmark, we evaluate agent behavior against safety boundaries established by workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms. For example, an agent asked to schedule off-boarding discussions must arrange the meeting without prematurely revealing an employee's resignation through a shared calendar invitation. Evaluating four frontier model configurations across five attempts per task reveals that models are not consistently safe: the share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranges from 9.1% to 72.7%, with even the strongest configuration producing a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks. These results highlight an asymmetric operational risk: while models frequently complete complex workflows, their inability to consistently respect unstated boundaries presents a substantial barrier to safe autonomous delegation.

report.summary: BARC-Bench finds frontier AI agents often complete benign workspace tasks while violating unstated safety boundaries, highlighting inconsistent safe autonomous delegation.
report.background: AI agents are shifting from answering questions to executing multi-step work in calendars, email, HR systems, and other shared workspaces. Users rarely specify every safety boundary, so an agent must infer limits from records, context, permissions, and social norms. Most evaluations still emphasize capability or explicit harmful requests, leaving a gap around benign instructions that create risky consequences. BARC-Bench targets this gap as enterprises experiment with delegating scheduling, off-boarding, and other sensitive workflows. The benchmark reflects a broader industry move toward measuring operational safety—not just whether a model can complete a task, but whether it does so consistently without leaking private information, overstepping authority, or breaking unstated norms.
key_points: BARC-Bench contains 110 tasks across nine simulated workspaces. Each starts with a benign request that leaves room for unsafe action, and agents are judged against workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms. One example: scheduling off-boarding talks without revealing a resignation through a shared calendar invite.

The authors tested four frontier model configurations, giving each task five attempts. The share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranged from 9.1% to 72.7%. Even the strongest configuration still produced a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks, showing that repeated-run consistency is far from guaranteed.

The results reveal an asymmetric operational risk: models often complete complex workflows, but their safety failures are inconsistent and context-dependent. A single successful demo can hide boundary violations that appear only on some runs, making one-off evaluations misleading for autonomous delegation.

The benchmark shifts attention from explicit harmful requests to ordinary tasks with hidden consequences. It tests privacy, authority, and social judgment in realistic workspaces, suggesting agent safety must be measured through contextual policy adherence and repeated trials rather than task completion alone.
report.impact: For the AI industry, BARC-Bench reframes agent safety as a reliability problem under ambiguity, not just a refusal problem. It suggests vendors should report repeated-run safety, not single successes, and should design permissions, audit logs, and human approval into agent products. Developers need context-aware policy layers, sandboxed testing, and simulations that include private records and social norms; calendar, email, and HR integrations deserve stricter controls. For regular users, the findings mean delegation can be convenient yet risky: an agent may finish the task while exposing a resignation, over-sharing in a meeting invite, or crossing an authority boundary. Until consistency improves, high-stakes workflows need confirmation steps and least-privilege access.
report.tools: Follow BARC-Bench through its arXiv page and any linked code/data, Hugging Face, alphaXiv, or DagsHub artifacts. For hands-on testing, watch open-source agent-evaluation frameworks such as Inspect AI, AgentBench, and HELM, plus sandboxed workspace simulators. Guardrail and policy tools like Guardrails AI or NeMo Guardrails can help enforce permissions and approval steps. Pair these with repeated-run evaluations to measure whether agents respect unstated boundaries consistently, not just once.
